items.ask: Define the deformation gradient F and state the physical meaning of J = det F.
items.answer: F = ∂x/∂X maps a reference line element to its current image: dx = F dX. J = det F = dv/dV is the local volume ratio, and J > 0 preserves orientation (matter keeps its handedness).
items.cue: F ferries fibres from X to x. J is the jar: current volume over reference volume.

items.ask: Give the physical meaning of a diagonal and an off-diagonal component of the small strain tensor.
items.answer: ε₁₁ is the extension per unit length of a fibre along x₁. ε₁₂ is half the engineering shear γ₁₂, where γ₁₂ is the decrease in the right angle between fibres along x₁ and x₂.
items.cue: Diagonal stretches, off-diagonal is half the angle drop: γ = 2ε.

items.ask: State the Voigt ordering of the strain vector and which entries carry a factor 2.
items.answer: Order 11, 22, 33, 23, 13, 12. Strain vector [ε₁₁, ε₂₂, ε₃₃, 2ε₂₃, 2ε₁₃, 2ε₁₂], so the shear entries are engineering strains γ. The stress vector holds σ₂₃, σ₁₃, σ₁₂ directly, so σ·ε gives the work correctly.
items.cue: Count down the diagonal, then 23, 13, 12 (skip the index you lack). Shears double into γ.

items.ask: In the polar decomposition F = RU = VR, what are R, U and V and what do they share?
items.answer: R is a proper orthogonal rotation. U is the right stretch tensor (acts in the reference configuration), V the left stretch tensor (acts in the current configuration). U and V are symmetric positive definite with the same eigenvalues, the principal stretches.
items.cue: Read right to left: RU stretches then rotates, VR rotates then stretches. Same stretches, different frames.

items.ask: State the conditions under which small strain theory replaces Green-Lagrange strain.
items.answer: The displacement gradient is small, |Grad u| ≪ 1, so both strains and rotations are small. Then the quadratic term HᵀH is negligible, E ≈ ε, and reference and current configurations coincide for writing equilibrium.
items.cue: Small gradient H: H + Hᵀ dominates HᵀH. Small rotation as well as small strain.

items.ask: What do the compatibility equations guarantee, and how many are there in 2D and 3D?
items.answer: They guarantee that a strain field derives from a single-valued, continuous displacement field (simply connected body). One equation in 2D, six Saint-Venant equations in 3D (three independent).
items.cue: Six strains, three displacements: the strains must mesh like puzzle pieces. 2D: one equation, 3D: six.

items.ask: Give the stretch and the Green strain of a material fibre with reference unit direction N.
items.answer: λ = √(N·CN) with C = FᵀF. The Green strain of that fibre is E_NN = N·EN = ½(λ² − 1).
items.cue: C measures squared length: λ² = N·CN. Green strain is half the change in squared length.

items.ask: For a rigid rotation F = R by angle θ, what are the Green-Lagrange strain E and the small strain ε?
items.answer: C = RᵀR = I, so E = 0 exactly for any rotation. The small strain ε = ½(R + Rᵀ) − I has in-plane diagonal entries cos θ − 1 ≈ −θ²/2, a second-order error, so ε is accurate for small rotations.
items.cue: Green is rotation-proof because RᵀR = I. Linear strain sees cos θ − 1, which is order θ².

items.ask: With t = σn, what does the component σᵢⱼ represent?
items.answer: tᵢ = σᵢⱼnⱼ, so σᵢⱼ is the i-component of traction on the face with outward normal eⱼ. Symmetry σᵢⱼ = σⱼᵢ makes the two index readings equal.
items.cue: Contract the normal into the second index: the free first index is the force direction.

items.ask: Which balance law makes the Cauchy stress symmetric, and under what assumption?
items.answer: Balance of angular momentum, assuming zero distributed body couples and couple stresses (a nonpolar continuum). The local result is σ = σᵀ.
items.cue: Shrink a cube: the moments of the shear pairs must balance, so τ_xy = τ_yx.

items.ask: List the steps of the Cauchy tetrahedron argument.
items.answer: 1) Tetrahedron with three faces on coordinate planes and a slanted face with normal n, area ΔA. 2) Face areas ΔAᵢ = nᵢΔA. 3) Body force and inertia scale with volume hΔA/3. 4) Let h → 0: surface forces balance, giving t(n) = σn.
items.cue: Volume terms shrink faster than area terms: as h → 0, only tractions survive, and t is linear in n.

items.ask: Define principal stresses and principal directions.
items.answer: They are the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of σ: σn = s n. On a principal plane the traction is purely normal (zero shear). For symmetric σ the three values are real and the directions mutually orthogonal.
items.cue: Principal plane: traction points straight along the normal. Symmetric matrix: real eigenvalues, orthogonal eigenvectors.

items.ask: State the maximum in-plane and absolute maximum shear stress and the orientation of the max shear plane.
items.answer: In-plane: τ_max = (σ₁ − σ₂)/2, the Mohr circle radius, on planes at 45° to the principal directions. Absolute: (σ_max − σ_min)/2 over all three principal stresses.
items.cue: Radius of the biggest Mohr circle. 45° in the body is 90° on the circle.

items.ask: Under a superposed rigid motion x* = Q(t)x + c(t), how do F, C, B and σ transform?
items.answer: F* = QF, C* = C (unchanged), B* = QBQᵀ, σ* = QσQᵀ. Objective vectors transform as v* = Qv and objective tensors as A* = QAQᵀ.
items.cue: Q joins F on the left, so C = FᵀF swallows QᵀQ = I while B and σ get sandwiched.

items.ask: Define the hydrostatic and deviatoric parts of stress and link them to von Mises.
items.answer: Mean stress σ_m = tr σ/3. Deviator s = σ − σ_m I, with tr s = 0. J₂ = ½ s:s, and σ_vm = √(3J₂). Hydrostatic stress changes volume; the deviator drives shape change and yield in metals.
items.cue: Split into a balloon part (pressure) and a twist part (deviator). Metals yield on the twist part.

items.ask: Write the three stress invariants in terms of principal stresses.
items.answer: I₁ = σ₁ + σ₂ + σ₃, I₂ = σ₁σ₂ + σ₂σ₃ + σ₃σ₁, I₃ = σ₁σ₂σ₃.
items.cue: Sum, sum of pair products, product: the coefficients of (s − σ₁)(s − σ₂)(s − σ₃).

items.ask: How do you impose a traction boundary condition on an inclined face?
items.answer: Write the unit outward normal n of the face, then set σn = t̄ at every point of the face (t̄ = 0 for a free face). In 2D that gives two scalar equations.
items.cue: Free face: σn = 0 along the slanted normal, both components, pointwise.

items.ask: Define the bulk modulus and give it in terms of E, ν and of λ, μ.
items.answer: Under hydrostatic pressure σ = −pI, K = −p/(ΔV/V) = −p/tr ε: the resistance to volume change. K = E/(3(1 − 2ν)) = λ + 2μ/3.
items.cue: Squeeze a sponge evenly: pressure per unit volume strain. ν → ½ sends K to infinity.

items.ask: Derive K = E/(3(1 − 2ν)) from isotropic Hooke's law.
items.answer: Apply σ = −pI. Compliance: ε = ((1 + ν)/E)(−p)I − (ν/E)(−3p)I = −p(1 − 2ν)/E · I. Then tr ε = −3p(1 − 2ν)/E, and K = −p/tr ε = E/(3(1 − 2ν)).
items.cue: (1 + ν) − 3ν = 1 − 2ν, times three directions for the trace.

items.ask: State the admissible range of Poisson's ratio for an isotropic solid and typical values.
items.answer: −1 < ν < ½, from G > 0 and K > 0 with E > 0. Metals about 0.3, rubber about 0.4999 (nearly incompressible), cork about 0.
items.cue: G = E/(2(1 + ν)) fixes the floor at −1, K = E/(3(1 − 2ν)) fixes the ceiling at ½.

items.ask: How many independent elastic constants for anisotropic, orthotropic, transversely isotropic, cubic and isotropic materials?
items.answer: General anisotropic 21, orthotropic 9, transversely isotropic 5, cubic 3, isotropic 2.
items.cue: 21, 9, 5, 3, 2: more symmetry, fewer constants.

items.ask: State the symmetries of Cᵢⱼₖₗ and where each comes from.
items.answer: Minor symmetries Cᵢⱼₖₗ = Cⱼᵢₖₗ = Cᵢⱼₗₖ from symmetry of σ and ε (81 → 36). Major symmetry Cᵢⱼₖₗ = Cₖₗᵢⱼ from the existence of a strain energy W (36 → 21).
items.cue: Minor: swap within a pair. Major: swap the pairs, because C = ∂²W/∂ε∂ε.

items.ask: What conditions on the Lamé constants make the isotropic strain energy positive definite?
items.answer: μ > 0 and 3λ + 2μ > 0, equivalently G > 0 and K > 0.
items.cue: Energy splits into a shear part (μ) and a volume part (K = λ + 2μ/3): both must be positive.

items.ask: What does isotropy imply for the stiffness tensor and for principal axes?
items.answer: Material response is the same in every direction: C is invariant under every rotation, leaving two constants (λ, μ). Principal axes of stress and strain coincide.
items.cue: Spin the sample, same answer. Two constants, coaxial σ and ε.

items.ask: What happens to K, λ, μ and E as ν → ½?
items.answer: K → ∞ and λ → ∞ while μ stays finite and E → 3μ. Volume change goes to zero, and pressure becomes a reaction (Lagrange multiplier) set by equilibrium and boundary conditions.
items.cue: Incompressible: only shear stiffness μ remains; E = 2μ(1 + ½) = 3μ.

items.ask: Under uniaxial stress σ, give the axial strain, lateral strain and volumetric strain.
items.answer: ε₁₁ = σ/E, ε₂₂ = ε₃₃ = −νσ/E, and ε_v = tr ε = (1 − 2ν)σ/E.
items.cue: One stretch, two equal contractions of ν each: volume factor 1 − 2ν.

items.ask: Define plane stress and give the out-of-plane strain.
items.answer: σ₁₃ = σ₂₃ = σ₃₃ = 0: a thin plate loaded in its plane, free faces. The plate thins or thickens with ε₃₃ = −(ν/E)(σ₁₁ + σ₂₂).
items.cue: Thin sheet, faces free, so the third stress row is zero and the thickness strain is free.

items.ask: Define plane strain, give where it applies and the out-of-plane stress.
items.answer: ε₁₃ = ε₂₃ = ε₃₃ = 0: a long prismatic body with constrained ends and loads uniform along its length (dam, tunnel, thick pipe). Then σ₃₃ = ν(σ₁₁ + σ₂₂).
items.cue: Long body, ends held: the third strain row is zero and σ₃₃ carries ν times the in-plane sum.

items.ask: List the steps of the Airy stress function method.
items.answer: 1) Pick φ with ∇⁴φ = 0 (polynomial or polar form). 2) Get stresses from the Airy definitions. 3) Impose traction BCs: pointwise on long edges, resultants on short ends (Saint-Venant). 4) Strains via Hooke, integrate for displacements, fix rigid body terms.
items.cue: Pick, differentiate, match edges, integrate: φ → σ → BCs → u.

items.ask: Where does ∇⁴φ = 0 come from in the Airy method?
items.answer: The Airy definitions satisfy equilibrium identically (zero body force). Substituting the stresses into Hooke's law and then into the 2D compatibility equation gives ∇⁴φ = 0.
items.cue: Equilibrium is built into φ; compatibility is the equation φ must solve.

items.ask: State Saint-Venant's principle.
items.answer: Statically equivalent load distributions (same resultant force and moment) produce stress fields that differ appreciably only within a distance of about the largest cross-section dimension from the loaded region.
items.cue: Far from the grip, the beam feels only the resultant. Decay length about one depth.

items.ask: Which polynomial Airy functions are automatically biharmonic, and what stress fields do degrees 2 and 3 give?
items.answer: All terms of degree 3 or lower satisfy ∇⁴φ = 0 automatically. Degree 2 gives uniform stress; degree 3 gives stress linear in x, y (pure bending). Degree 4 and higher need relations among coefficients.
items.cue: Four derivatives annihilate a cubic. Stress order = φ order − 2.

items.ask: Give the stress concentration factor at a circular hole in an infinite plate under uniaxial, equibiaxial and pure shear loading.
items.answer: Uniaxial σ₀: K_t = 3 (σ_θθ = 3σ₀ at the edge points on the diameter perpendicular to the load). Equibiaxial: 2. Pure shear τ: 4.
items.cue: Superpose two uniaxial Kirsch fields: same signs give 3 − 1 = 2, opposite signs (shear) give 3 + 1 = 4.

items.ask: Give the general axisymmetric Airy function and the resulting stresses when displacement is single valued.
items.answer: φ = A ln r + B r² ln r + C r² + D. Single-valued displacement requires B = 0, giving σ_rr = A/r² + 2C and σ_θθ = −A/r² + 2C (the Lamé form).
items.cue: ln r gives ±A/r², r² gives uniform 2C. Equal and opposite 1/r² terms in radial and hoop.

items.ask: When is the thin-walled vessel theory valid, and what do you do when a design result violates it?
items.answer: Valid for r/t ≥ 10: stress uniform through the wall and σ_r (order p) small compared with σ_θ (order pr/t). When the required t comes out comparable to r (say t = D/4), state that the thin-wall assumption is violated and switch to Lamé.
items.cue: Thin wall: r/t at least 10. A thick answer means a broken premise: say so, then use Lamé.

items.ask: Derive the hoop and axial stresses of a thin cylinder from free body cuts.
items.answer: Hoop: cut along a diameter, length L: 2σ_θ t L = p(2r)L, so σ_θ = pr/t. Axial: cut across the tube: σ_z(2πrt) = pπr², so σ_z = pr/(2t).
items.cue: Pressure acts on the projected area: 2rL for the hoop cut, πr² for the end cap.

items.ask: For the same p, r and allowable stress, compare the wall thickness of a thin sphere and a thin cylinder.
items.answer: The sphere needs half the cylinder's thickness, since its stress pr/(2t) equals the cylinder's axial stress, half the hoop stress pr/t.
items.cue: Sphere: every direction is axial. Half the stress, half the wall.

items.ask: State the boundary conditions for a thick cylinder with inner radius a, outer radius b, internal pressure p_i and external pressure p_o.
items.answer: σ_rr(a) = −p_i and σ_rr(b) = −p_o (tension positive, so pressure is compressive radial stress). Two equations fix the Lamé constants A and B.
items.cue: Pressure pushes into the wall: radial stress equals minus the pressure on each surface.

items.ask: For a thick cylinder under internal pressure p only, give the bore hoop stress and the maximum in-plane shear stress.
items.answer: At r = a: σ_θθ = p(b² + a²)/(b² − a²), σ_rr = −p. Maximum in-plane shear at the bore: (σ_θθ − σ_rr)/2 = pb²/(b² − a²).
items.cue: Bore is critical. Thin limit b → a: hoop approaches pr/t, matching the thin formula.

items.ask: Give σ_zz in a thick cylinder under internal pressure p for open ends, closed ends and axially restrained ends.
items.answer: Open ends: σ_zz = 0. Closed ends: σ_zz = pa²/(b² − a²) = A. Restrained ends (plane strain): σ_zz = ν(σ_rr + σ_θθ) = 2νA = 2νpa²/(b² − a²). All uniform through the wall.
items.cue: σ_rr + σ_θθ = 2A is constant, so every end condition gives a uniform σ_zz.

items.ask: Write the axisymmetric radial equilibrium equations for a cylinder and a sphere.
items.answer: Cylinder: dσ_rr/dr + (σ_rr − σ_θθ)/r = 0. Sphere: dσ_rr/dr + 2(σ_rr − σ_θθ)/r = 0 (two equal hoop directions). Zero body force in both.
items.cue: The factor counts hoop directions: one for the cylinder, two for the sphere, hence B/r² versus B/r³.

items.ask: What is the stress state at the bore of a thick sphere under internal pressure, and which Lamé form applies?
items.answer: Equibiaxial hoop tension σ_θθ = σ_φφ plus radial compression σ_rr = −p. The sphere uses σ_rr = A − B/r³, σ_θθ = A + B/(2r³), from 3D spherical equilibrium (Airy is a plane construct).
items.cue: Sphere: 1/r³ and the half on the hoop term. Two equal hoops plus a radial push at the bore.

items.ask: Give the centre stress of a solid spinning disc (plane stress) of outer radius b and the feature of its solution method.
items.answer: σ_rr = σ_θθ = (3 + ν)ρω²b²/8 at the centre, the maximum. The body force ρω²r requires a particular solution added to the Lamé homogeneous solution.
items.cue: Centrifugal load ρω²r drives a particular solution. (3 + ν)/8 at the hub, equal radial and hoop.

items.ask: Define a hyperelastic material and state the objectivity requirement on its energy.
items.answer: Stress derives from a strain energy W(F): P = ∂W/∂F, so the work done is path independent. Objectivity requires W to depend on F through C = FᵀF (W = W(C)).
items.cue: Energy first, stress by differentiation. Feed W the rotation-blind C.

items.ask: Name the three stress measures, their configurations, symmetry and work conjugates.
items.answer: Cauchy σ: current force per current area, symmetric, conjugate to D. First Piola-Kirchhoff P: current force per reference area, two-point and generally unsymmetric, conjugate to Ḟ. Second Piola-Kirchhoff S: fully referential, symmetric, conjugate to Ė.
items.cue: σ:D, P:Ḟ, S:Ė. P straddles both worlds; σ and S each live in one and are symmetric.

items.ask: State Nanson's formula.
items.answer: n da = J F⁻ᵀ N dA, relating a current oriented area to its reference counterpart.
items.cue: Same factor JF⁻ᵀ as in P = JσF⁻ᵀ, because t da = σn da = PN dA.

items.ask: What is the role of the pressure p in incompressible hyperelasticity?
items.answer: Incompressibility imposes J = 1. The pressure p is a Lagrange multiplier enforcing it: the constitutive law fixes the stress up to −pI, and p is found from equilibrium and boundary conditions.
items.cue: Constraint J = 1, multiplier p. Find p from a traction-free face.

items.ask: Outline the incompressible neo-Hookean uniaxial tension solution.
items.answer: Stretches λ, λ^(−1/2), λ^(−1/2) (J = 1). Principal stresses σᵢ = −p + μλᵢ². Free lateral faces: σ₂ = 0 gives p = μ/λ. Then σ₁₁ = μ(λ² − 1/λ) and nominal P₁₁ = σ₁₁/λ = μ(λ − 1/λ²).
items.cue: Volume locks the sides to λ^(−1/2); free sides set p; small strain gives 3με = Eε.

items.ask: Set up the thin incompressible spherical balloon under large deformation.
items.answer: Hoop stretches λ_θ = λ_φ = λ = R/R₀; radial stretch λ_r = t/t₀ = 1/λ². Neo-Hookean σᵢ = −p + μλᵢ². Thin wall σ_rr = 0 gives p = μλ⁻⁴, so σ_θθ = μ(λ² − λ⁻⁴). Sphere equilibrium: P = 2σ_θθ t/R.
items.cue: Two hoops stretch by λ, the wall thins by λ²; free radial direction sets p.

items.ask: Give the balloon inflation pressure versus stretch and the stretch at the pressure peak.
items.answer: P = 2μ(t₀/R₀)(λ⁻¹ − λ⁻⁷). dP/dλ = 0 gives λ⁶ = 7, λ = 7^(1/6) ≈ 1.38. Beyond this limit point pressure falls while radius grows: hard to start, then easier.
items.cue: Seven in the exponent, seven under the sixth root: λ_peak = 7^(1/6).

items.ask: For finite simple shear x₁ = X₁ + γX₂, give F, B and J.
items.cue: γ sits above the diagonal of F; B gains γ² in the 11 slot from the tilted X₂ fibres.

items.ask: For neo-Hookean finite simple shear with faces x₂ = const traction free in the normal direction, give the stresses and the meaning of τ/G.
items.answer: σ₂₂ = 0 gives p = μ. Then σ₁₂ = μγ, σ₁₁ = μγ², σ₂₂ = σ₃₃ = 0. τ/G = γ, the amount of shear (tangent of the shear angle). The normal stress μγ² is a second-order effect of finite shear (Poynting effect).
items.cue: Shear stays linear, μγ; normal stress appears at order γ², from B₁₁ = 1 + γ².

items.ask: What linear elastic constants does the neo-Hookean model reduce to at small strain?
items.answer: Shear modulus μ and ν = ½ (incompressible), so E = 3μ. For Mooney-Rivlin, μ = 2(C₁ + C₂).
items.cue: Small stretch λ = 1 + ε: μ(λ² − 1/λ) ≈ 3με, so E = 3μ.

items.ask: Define the Lagrangian and Eulerian descriptions of motion.
items.answer: Lagrangian (material, referential): fields are functions of X and t, following each particle. Eulerian (spatial): fields are functions of x and t, observed at fixed points in space.
items.cue: Lagrangian rides the boat with the particle; Eulerian stands on the bridge watching the river.

items.ask: Write the acceleration in the spatial description.
items.answer: a = Dv/Dt = ∂v/∂t + (grad v)v, the local rate plus the convective term.
items.cue: Steady flow through a nozzle still accelerates: the convective term (grad v)v does it.

items.ask: List the balance laws of continuum mechanics.
items.answer: 1) Conservation of mass. 2) Balance of linear momentum. 3) Balance of angular momentum. 4) Balance of energy (first law). 5) Entropy inequality (second law, Clausius-Duhem).
items.cue: M-L-A-E-S: Mass, Linear, Angular, Energy, entropy Second law.

items.ask: Define the rate of deformation D and spin W, and relate D to the Green strain rate.
items.answer: D = ½(L + Lᵀ) and W = ½(L − Lᵀ) with L = grad v. D measures stretching rate, W the spin. Ė = FᵀDF, and D = 0 everywhere means an instantaneously rigid motion.
items.cue: Same symmetric/skew split as ε and ω, now on velocity. Pull back D with Fᵀ( )F to get Ė.

items.ask: Give the steps from a global balance law to its local form.
items.answer: 1) Write the global balance for an arbitrary material region. 2) Convert surface integrals with the divergence theorem. 3) Bring the time derivative inside with Reynolds transport. 4) Collect into one volume integral equal to zero. 5) Region arbitrary and integrand continuous, so the integrand vanishes pointwise.
items.cue: Global, divergence, Reynolds, combine, localize: an integral that is zero over every region has a zero integrand.

items.ask: State three equivalent conditions for an isochoric (incompressible) motion.
items.answer: div v = 0, J̇ = 0 (J = 1 throughout), and Dρ/Dt = 0 (density constant following each particle).
items.cue: J̇ = J div v and ρJ = ρ₀ tie all three together.

items.ask: Write the stress power per unit reference volume using each conjugate pair.
items.answer: Jσ:D = P:Ḟ = S:Ė. Per unit current volume, the stress power is σ:D.
items.cue: Every pair gives the same power; J converts current volume to reference volume.

items.ask: State the divergence theorem in the form used for traction in balance laws.
items.answer: ∫_∂Ω σn da = ∫_Ω div σ dv, in index form ∫ σᵢⱼnⱼ da = ∫ σᵢⱼ,ⱼ dv.
items.cue: Contract the normal and the derivative on the same index j.

items.ask: Describe the free thermal strain of an isotropic solid and when thermal stress arises.
items.answer: ε_th = αΔT I: equal normal strain in all directions, zero shear. Uniform heating of an unconstrained body gives zero stress. Stress arises from external constraint or from a nonuniform temperature field.
items.cue: Free and uniform: it grows evenly and stays stress free. Hold it or heat it unevenly to make stress.

items.ask: Give the thermal stress for a bar, an in-plane restrained plate and a fully restrained block heated by ΔT.
items.answer: Bar: σ = −EαΔT. Plate: σ = −EαΔT/(1 − ν). Block: σ = −EαΔT/(1 − 2ν) = −3KαΔT. Each added restrained direction raises the compression.
items.cue: Divisors 1, 1 − ν, 1 − 2ν: the more directions held, the bigger the push back.

items.ask: State the Voigt and Reuss estimates for a two-phase composite and which bound each gives.
items.answer: Voigt (equal strain, parallel): M = Σ fᵢMᵢ, the upper bound. Reuss (equal stress, series): 1/M = Σ fᵢ/Mᵢ, the lower bound. Particles in a matrix under uniform pressure, 1/k_eff = (1 − f)/k_A + f/k_B, is the Reuss lower bound.
items.cue: Parallel springs add stiffness (upper); series springs add compliance (lower). True value sits between.

items.ask: List the assumptions behind the longitudinal rule of mixtures E₁ = V_fE_f + V_mE_m.
items.answer: Perfect fibre-matrix bonding, equal axial strain in fibre and matrix, both linear elastic, load shared in proportion to area (volume) fractions, and continuous aligned fibres.
items.cue: Glued side by side and pulled together: same strain, forces add by area.

items.ask: How many independent in-plane elastic constants describe an orthotropic ply in plane stress, and which?
items.answer: Four: E₁, E₂, ν₁₂, G₁₂. ν₂₁ follows from reciprocity ν₂₁ = ν₁₂E₂/E₁.
items.cue: Two moduli, one Poisson ratio, one shear modulus; reciprocity supplies the fifth symbol.

items.ask: Define ν₁₂ for an orthotropic ply.
items.answer: ν₁₂ = −ε₂/ε₁ under uniaxial stress σ₁: load along direction 1, contraction measured in direction 2.
items.cue: First index: the load direction. Second index: the contraction direction.

items.ask: Give the meaning of the A, B, D matrices and the laminate layups that simplify them.
items.answer: A: extensional stiffness (in-plane forces from midplane strains). B: extension-bending coupling, zero for a symmetric laminate. D: bending stiffness. A₁₆ = A₂₆ = 0 for a balanced laminate (each +θ paired with −θ).
items.cue: Symmetric kills B; balanced kills A₁₆, A₂₆. Weights 1, z, z².

items.ask: Which mechanism governs the longitudinal compressive strength of a unidirectional carbon fibre ply?
items.answer: Fibre microbuckling (kink banding) of the slender fibres, supported only by the compliant matrix. Compressive strength is therefore well below the fibre-dominated tensile strength.
items.cue: Picture uncooked spaghetti in jelly: pull it and the strands carry load; push it and they kink.
